text: This is an AI scientist for GPU rental prices. It forecasts thirty-seven posted GPU prices one, three and seven days ahead, and tests which kinds of AI help make those forecasts better on data the system has not seen.
Each published price is the middle of a list of offers. So we asked two questions. Does looking at the whole list beat looking at the median alone? And which kinds of AI help survive a fair test?

The headline. The forecast we hand in made twenty percent less error than drift, the reference forecast, on days no model had seen. That is every forecaster, scored on the same four hundred and seventy-nine fresh forecasts.
The key insight. Two thirds of the movement in a published median comes from offers joining or leaving the list, not from providers changing their prices.
So our engine replays what each offer did on past days, applies that to today's list, and takes the middle again. The spread of those replayed middles is the forecast range.
Here it is step by step. Offers reprice, leave, or rejoin. Each replay gives a new median, and together they form the forecast.
On top of the engine sit five AI agents, each with one job: a list reader, a repricer watcher, a base-rate keeper, a reference weigher and a jump spotter. Their forecasts are averaged.

Training is a recursive self-improvement loop. Each round, the crowd forecasts practice days and a verifier scores it. A coach AI proposes one change. A second verifier keeps it only if practice days improve and hidden check days do not get worse. The verifiers are fixed code the AI cannot change. Ten rounds, then a final exam on unseen days: four percent better than the first crowd.
At inference the crowd is frozen. For each price, the five agents read the facts, their answers are averaged, and the ranges are stretched. One pass per price, one hundred and eleven forecasts.
The test was written down before the results existed: a committed protocol, a time machine that only sees past data, shuffled worlds as a placebo, and exam days no model had seen.
Across three separate tests, the engine beat drift by about eight percent, and the five agents by fifteen to nineteen percent.

Not every idea worked. Of seven ways to make the system improve itself, two held up: the coach, and reinforcement learning that teaches a small model to forecast. Three did not, and two were not established.
One honest caveat. Ranges held the truth eighty percent of the time overall, but only sixty-six percent of the time when the price actually moved.

Three things to remember. Look inside the list. Five AI agents plus a coach cut error by twenty percent on unseen days. And most self-improvement ideas fail a fair test. The verifier is what makes the loop trustworthy.
